PETITION RESPECTING PROPOSED DEMOLITION OF ROXBOROUGH APARTMENTS AND UNION STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, exercising the ancient right of the citizen, I wish to present a petition to the Honourable House of Commons, in Parliament assembled, on behalf of the tenants and staff of the Roxborough Apartments, with respect to the proposed demolition of the Roxborough and the Union Station by the National Capital Commission.
Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray that your Honourable House may be pleased to reconsider the plans for the Roxborough's and Union Station's demolition in the name of civic progress and capital re-development. We are confident that many citizens of our capital city would concur and support this presentation.
And as in duty bound your petitioners will ever pray.

subsubtopic: SOUTHERN RHODESIA-CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs on a matter of great importance to all Commonwealth statesmen, a matter which the British Prime Minister yesterday indicated was being discussed by Commonwealth Governments. Is the Minister in a position to indicate what is to be Canada's attitude toward Rhodesian independence and the discussions with respect thereto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: SOUTHERN RHODESIA-CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am. The Government has made clear on a number of occasions our view that a unilateral declaration of independence by the Rhodesian Government would be a deplorable act which would lead to very serious economic and internal political difficulties in Rhodesia. Moreover, we think the repercussions throughout Africa, particularly on race relations, might be serious. We have conveyed our views to the Rhodesian Government. We earnestly hope that the Southern Rhodesian Government will take no such action. We have of course paid particular attention to the statement made yesterday in the British House of Commons.
In his statement in this House on July 17, 1964, following the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' meeting, the Prime Minister indicated that Canada would not recognize the validity of a unilateral declaration of independence by the Rhodesian Government. If
April 30, 1965

Inquiries of the Ministry such a declaration took place we would have to consider other measures, in consultation with other Commonwealth Governments.
I should, however, add that negotiations on independence between the British and Rhodesian Governments are still going on. I hope they will eventually result in agreement on a program which will lead to independence for Rhodesia within the Commonwealth, in the words of the communique issued by the Prime Ministers' Conference, "at the earliest practical time on the basis of majority rule".

On the orders of the day:
Kon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I undertook yesterday to provide answers to two questions asked by the hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich.
In answer to his first question, to the best of my knowledge the Government has not received any communication from the Government of British Columbia or from the Premier of that Province in respect to the using up of the Provincial quota of the municipal development and loan fund.
The second question concerned a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the House during the second reading of the Municipal Development and Loan bill on August 2, 1963. At that time the question had to do with the possibility that provincial quotas might be used up before the closing date of March 31, 1966, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a general reply to the effect that under certain circumstances the Government would not hesitate to come back to Parliament-and I quote his words- "to be sure that the purposes of the Act are fulfilled". That is the end of the quotation.
I think it would be agreed that the purposes of the Act have been met in a most satisfactory manner. An examination of the record will show that during the passage of the legislation I and other spokesmen for the Government made frequent references to the fact that the municipal development and loan fund was a short term measure intended to promote a rapid increase in municipal construction and employment during the next two years following the passage of the legislation. It now appears that the $400 million fund will be almost completely used up by
April 30, 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry the terminal date of the legislation on March 31 next. No decision has been made by the Government to increase the amount of funds available.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, April 29, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on the budget with regard to which I should like to give my views on a few subjects.
First of all I wish to refer to the field of education. I was somewhat disappointed that during the budget speech the Minister of Finance did not see fit, in the interim between now and the report of the Bladen Commission, to do something at the Federal level in the field of education. It is clear that at the present time education is the most costly service in Canada for all Governments. It involves the highest spending outlay.
The Economic Council of Canada feels that in the future education will continue to be the greatest expense, and that the margin is going to increase rapidly as time goes on. In 1963 total Government expenditures were over $2 billion, which was $90 million higher than the next highest figure for Government expenditure. The Economic Council of Canada expects that by 1970 this figure will reach $3 billion.
This figure represents only two thirds of the total cost for higher education. At present the real burden of higher education does not fall on the Federal Government. This is primarily a provincial field, as I know and as other Members have mentioned. The share of the Federal Government in 1962 was $59 million out of a total of $266 million spent by all Governments on higher education, or just under 25 per cent of total expenditures. Out of the $59 million spent by the Federal Government for higher education in 1962, $26 million was in the form of research grants to the National Research Council.
The Provinces and the Municipalities bear the great load with regard to expenditures for education, and the municipal burden has now reached the point of bankrupting municipalities. Mill rates are soaring, and the largest percentage of these rates goes for education. For example, in Ontario education requires approximately 50 per cent of

municipal tax revenues, and education now accounts for over 47 per cent of the Ontario provincial budget.
The Minister of Finance stated during the budget speech that he was waiting for the report of the Bladen Commission before doing anything for higher education, but the fact is that the Canadian Universities Foundation, which was responsible for setting up the Bladen Commission, recommended to the Minister of Finance in 1963 that the per capita grant should be brought in line with student enrolment and operating costs. Today that would mean a $3 per capita grant. I should like to quote the following from the Regina Leader-Post of April 27:
Mr. Thatcher expressed concern about progress in the field of education unless the Federal Government can find some way of increasing financial aid for technical sohools and universities.
The former premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Lloyd, said:
The ignoring of the needs of education is "a far cry from Mr. Gordon's statement of last year when he said mere selected and long term measures are needed such as the better education and technical training of our people". Both the Federal and Provincial Government have failed to recognize the contributions education makes to the expansion of the economy, estimated by some economists to range from 20 to 40 per cent.
The Federal grant last year for higher education was $27 million, but the trouble is it is calculated on a per capita basis per province and, as other Members have pointed out, the per capita increase in population is less rapid. The per capita increase in population of a province is about 2 per cent, while the per student increase across the country averages between 11 per cent and 12 per cent, and the student population is increasing at a progressively faster rate each year. In addition the operating costs of the universities are increasing even more rapidly, by 16 per cent each year. So we can say that while student enrolment and especially operating costs are increasing, they are not nearly being met by the per capita increase on which the grant is based. So what has happened is that the grant per student or per operating cost has diminished each year, and the real value of the grant is diminishing rapidly.
This grant should be calculated on a per student basis. On the present basis the grant to the Province of Saskatchewan for the year 1962-63 was $269, and by 1964-65 it had fallen to $199. So the real value of the grant to the student is rapidly diminishing. The figure for Saskatchewan is away below the
April 30. 1965

national average and is actually the third lowest in Canada. The population of Saskatchewan has not been increasing for many years. We hope that at the present time it will start to increase. It used to be said that one of the greatest exports from Saskatchewan was people when it should have been wheat, and we hope this condition will now be alleviated.
With regard to enrolment of full time students at universities, in 1954-55 they represented 4.4 per cent of young people in the 18 to 24 age group. However, by 1964-65 this figure had risen to over 9 per cent, and it is estimated by the Canadian Universities Foundation that full time students will represent over 15 per cent by the year 1974-75, and this is probably a low estimation. This is the probable expansion. Some 15 years ago the United States had over 8 per cent of that age range in universities, and today they have close to 40 per cent.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
University fees have been skyrocketing. I think we are moving in the direction of providing free education. The Canadian Union of Students has asked for free tuition in its recent brief to the Bladen Commission. I believe the Prime Minister went so far as to endorse free education. Fees, however, are really a very small part of the cost of education, since they form only about one quarter to one fifth of the cost to the student.
What should the Federal Government do about this? If Governments do not make money available to cover the rise in the cost of education, then the universities will have to draw from the only source they control, and that is fees. The student will then bear the cost of the Government's failure to meet this need. A rise in fees is the only other alternative, and they will go up and up.
Federal spending in direct grants to higher education during 1964-65 amounted to only one third of 1 per cent of total spending. This is ludicrous and should not continue. If we expect the provinces to bear almost the full cost of primary and secondary education, then the Federal Government must take more responsibility and must give much more for higher education in this country.
In conjunction with the subject of education I want to talk about health services from a national point of view. Both education and health services are investments; they are not handouts. I should like to stress that point. They represent real investments in the advance of mankind in every sphere. They will
The Budget-Mrs. Jones pay off on a dollar and cents basis. Some of the European countries in which a very high percentage of the national income goes into Government have also very productive economies. Both education and health needs are urgent in Canada now. They must progress together; they must advance hand in hand for the universal benefit of all Canadian people regardless of income.
I do not object to the term "war on poverty". I used it myself in my maiden speech last July. However, if it is to mean anything it must be an actual war carried on with effective weapons. It must not be allowed to wax and wane in a skirmish that is purely vocal, evasive and ineffective. In other words this must not be a phony war. Some people have drawn back in a state of apprehension and are paralysed by their fear that if a national program of health services is implemented, the funds needed in the field of education cannot be provided. Some are fearful that we cannot have either. Truly this is a time, I suppose, to excite the daring and test the strong. A society, in order to be healthy, must advance on all fronts. This must be a total war.
When I use the word "health", I mean not only a literal interpretation of that word. I am thinking of it in its broadest sense. For the benefit of those who are somewhat fearful may I point out, as the Minister of Finance has already pointed out, that the nation's finances are under firm control. This is nice to know; it is very encouraging. The expected increase in the gross national product will provide the revenue needed in both the education and health fields. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has asked Canadians to "think big." Well, that is fine; that is very encouraging. I would assume that this approach presages an aggressive export policy, because this also must be included. I shall not make the mistake of including wheat sales in this particular outlook, because I understand that would be inappropriate.
I should like to quote from the Star-Phoenix in this regard. The editorial is dated April 12, 1965 and is under the caption "What about the next budget?"
Presuming taxes will be slashed-
This is an overestimation of what actually happened.
-the welfare program can be pursued on the assumption that the gross national product, the sum total of goods and services produced, will expand sufficiently to pay for the welfare spending spree.
April 30, 1965

The Budget-Mrs. Jones
I should like to interject here that I do not really feel that Federal funds devoted to the advance of education and health services could come within the definition of a "spending spree". As I pointed out, I feel they are absolutely necessary. I continue with the quotation:
A dramatic growth in the GNP would depend directly on establishing new Canadian export records...
If we have any hope of reaching the targets determined on by the Economic Council of Canada, then we must puli out all the stops. Canada must expand production for domestic and foreign consumption, it must look to an intensification of trade with Russia and Communist China.
If there is any wheat sale to Russia in the offing, we will all cheer for the Wheat Board. I continue the quotation:
In addition, Canada must embark on extended trading relations with the emerging nations, and it must face up to the protectionism of the European Common Market which threatens to hurt us deeply in the long run.
In the Throne speech, relatively little attention was given to Canada's greatest challenge-the promotion of a huge growth in exports. Without that, many of the major goals set by the Economic Council of Canada will prove meaningless. [DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
Those who shrink from tax increases resulting from the implementation of a universal national health service are not generally the people who have been hit hard by severe, prolonged illness, either mental or physical. The parent of a retarded child, the parent, wife, husband or any relative of an acutely mentally disturbed person, the relative of a handicapped person who is vegetating either in a home or an institution-ask those people how they feel about an increased expenditure of public funds for more effective research and more rehabilitation. I was listening to the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands when he was talking about the subject of taxation. I agree with him that none of us would object to higher taxation for these areas that have such a high priority and in which there is such a need at present in Canada. The time has come when something concrete has to be started in an organized way to provide assistance for people who need help. Next year or the year after will not do.
I wish to quote from the foreword to volume II of the report of the Royal Commission on Health Services:
We emphasized in volume I and we wish to repeat here that time is of the essence in the development of certain health services such as the implementation of crash programs for the education and training of health personnel, the expansion and organization of health research, the introdution of children's dental programs and

the provision of expanded health services for retarded and crippled children. Similar urgency applies to the expansion of the scope of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, particularly the inclusion of mental health hospital services under the coverage of that act.
This will be a good interim measure. Mental hospitals are currently being emptied. The patient population at the mental hospital in Weyburn reached an all time high of 2,600 back in the 1940's. When I arrived there on staff in 1950 it had a population of around 1,300, and has now reached an all time low of 800 patients.
The foreword to the Hall Commission report continues:
In fact we are heartened by the initiative shown by some of the provincial governments which are proceeding with the development of extensive programs of education and training of health personnel, and we refer particularly to the imaginative program involving $100 million announced recently by the Ontario government
In yesterday morning's Globe and Mail I noticed an item respecting the expansion of a research centre on the emotionally upset child. This is a $500,000 building program and is something that is very greatly needed.
I now return to the quotation from the Hall Report:
In other fields, no less important in the development of comprehensive and effective health services for all Canadians, haste should be made slowly because of the important long-term implications of the comprehensive programs which we have recommended. We visualize that full implementation of the programs may take seven years so that by 1971, Canadians would have all the health services which scientific genius and human skill can provide We have also presented evidence that given the continued economic expansion of our country, which is fully realizable, Canada will have the means in terms of qualified manpower, capital facilities and financing to undertake these programs without in any way interfering but, on the contrary, strengthening the economic capacity and growth prospects of our country.
I should now like to quote briefly from an editorial in the Toronto Star of January 30:
No one expects the federal Government to implement the Commission's report immediately; the Commission itself proposed that its recommendations should be brought into effect over a period of years.
But the Government should lose no time in making clear that it accepts the Royal Commission's report in principle and that it intends to take the preliminary steps for its establishment in the near future. Without at least that much guidance, provinces concerned with filling the medicare gap in the years immediately ahead may find themselves headed in the wrong direction.
That is an important point. Has the Federal Government in fact given the green light to the provinces to go ahead and start their own programs? Is it not going to give any
April 30, 1965

leadership on the national level for the provision of a health service program for Canada?
At the present time there are many areas in the health field that are crying out for help, for research, for improved care and for effective treatment. There are the mentally ill who have been the most neglected. There are the retarded children, the crippled children, people with debilitating diseases and our old people.
Excellent organizations like the Canadian Mental Health Association and the Canadian Association for Retarded Children have done much in the past to enlighten the public and give leadership in the care of the mentally ill and the retarded, but they cannot do it alone. In this year's estimates I notice that the Department of National Health and Welfare's grant to the Canadian Association for Retarded Children is raised from $15,000 to $25,000, but the Canadian Mental Health Association grant is still $15,000. I know every little bit helps, but what can a national health organization do to effectively wage the kind of war I have been describing, with princely sums like these?
I suppose they constitute a kind of governmental stamp of approval and evidence of continuing good will on the part of the Federal Government, but more concrete evidence of Government good will is required.
In preparation for the implementation of a national program of effective health services, all kinds of pilot projects need to be set up across the country. Since last fall I have been trying to get a grant for a pilot project, a community employment workshop, for those permanently and mentally handicapped in Saskatoon, which would provide a blueprint for community shelter workshops for people all across Canada who are permanently mentally helpless and who are classed as unemployable. All these people can do now is sit in complete idleness, living on relief and other government allowances. I found a great deal of interest and enthusiasm for this project among the people of Saskatoon. Surely the Federal Government should provide some leadership and sponsor pilot projects like this across the country.
Research projects carried on in Canada cannot always continue to rely on our neighbours to the south for the necessary funds to carry out their work. One psychiatrist on the staff of the University of Saskatchewan has for some years been carrying out a research program in the community partly
The Budget-Mrs. Jones financed by the provincial Government but to a larger extent by the United States Government. The National Institute of Mental Health in Washington has provided an annual grant of $20,000 on a three-year basis, and this year will provide an additional annual grant of $8,500 which will continue for the next three years. Both the N.I.M.H. grants from Washington and the private American foundation grants are going to dry up for us here in Canada. The Americans are beginning to say that we should finance our own research projects. Canada has something like one tenth of the population of the United States, and it is easier to do things on a broad basis and be able to validate them. The kind of research programs that could be carried out in Canada could provide an important Canadian contribution to the world, but at present in this whole field of research we are living on the largesse of our big brother down yonder. I think this helps destroy our sense of freedom, our sense of responsibility and our sense of identity.
The Minister of Finance seems very concerned about a sense of identity in Canada. He is thinking about protection for Canadian publications, and he wants to start the Canada Development Corporation, which goes along the same line of thinking in the sense of preserving our Canadian identity. In the century in which we live, with the great velocity of change in many fields, rapid advance in technology, increasing complexity in our society, governments becoming bigger and industries becoming bigger, people are tending to become more remote from participation in the affairs of their country. They do not participate as personally as they did, say 30 years ago, in questions of government, industry and many other spheres. Mr. Adlai Stevenson has referred to this whole question of the process of the alienation of the individual that exists in this world of ours at the present time by saying that man in this century does not need so much to fear becoming a slave as becoming a robot. This puts the whole thing in a nutshell.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
However, Mr. Speaker, there is a heartening kind of movement down at the grass roots in communities. In recent years people have been showing an increasing desire to take more responsibility, to express their concern in regard to all kinds of problems, social, health and welfare, educational; problems of business expansion, developmental problems of every kind. They have shown
788	COMMONS
The Budget-Mrs. Jones their desire to play a part in making decisions relating to their future well-being. This movement is counteracting this destructive mechanization of man, and is doing so in a very encouraging way; because we certainly need, in the latter part of this century, a kind of human renaissance that will parallel the rapid advances that have occurred in technology and other fields during the earlier part of this century. The voice of the individual is increasingly being directed to the ear of Governments, and this Government must heed and provide definite leadership and concrete encouragement in this interflow of communication.
Those who do research in our universities, hospitals and other community fields need to be given funds, freedom and security of tenure. At the time of the National Retardation Conference here last fall I was talking with the head of a training school in Saskatchewan, who told me that he had a great deal of trouble getting a research psychologist and holding him. On the last two occasions -as happens all the time-a research project had been started, and the research man hardly got settled in when he had to send a report justifying his program in order to get his grant for the next year. This kind of thing is discouraging. Grants provided on a yearly basis are just ludicrous from the standpoint of any kind of valuable research taking place. So these people were lost; one of them went to the United States. This is one of the reasons we have a brain drain out of this country.

Through you, Mr. Speaker, I want to thank hon. Members for this courtesy. I will be very brief. I want to say something about the removal of the tax on drugs. I noticed that the Minister of Finance decided that this matter should be referred to the Special Committee on Food and Drugs. This I found somewhat surprising, because I had felt that the consensus was that this tax should be removed. I do not know of anyone in this House who would oppose that. I put a question on the order paper last July, and the answer given was that it would be dealt with during the preparation of the budget.

DEBATES	April 30, 1965
I realize that the removal of the tax on drugs will not be any great bonanza and will really, practically, amount to only a few cents on the dollar. But this is something which is an added burden on people who are suffering illness and need medication, and I think the tax should be removed. This certainly could be done in the interim period before the recommendations of the Hall report in regard to prescription drug services are implemented. I would like to see this done, Mr. Speaker, and I do not quite know why the question was referred to the Special Committee on Food and Drugs.
At this point I want to speak very briefly on a subject that is of special interest to the people of Saskatoon at the present time. Parliament votes to give in the neighbourhood of $100 million a year to the C.B.C. This money comes out of the public purse; it is provided by the taxpayers. Recently, without reference to Parliament, an additional $10 million was allocated to the C.B.C. to provide an extra broadcasting centre for Expo '67.
I want to say something about the establishment of a C.B.C. channel in Saskatoon. The people of Saskatoon and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix want to know about this. From inquiries, I find that in June, 1963 an application was made by the C.B.C. for the reservation of a channel in Saskatoon. I believe at that time ten channels across Canada were under consideration. The Board of Broadcast Governors refused to consider the reservation of all these channels except two, one for Saskatoon and one for Saint John-Fred-ericton. I understand that at the request of the then Secretary of State, the present Minister of Transport, a troika committee was set up including Dr. Stewart, Mr. Jamieson, who was then President of the C.A.B., and Mr. Ouimet. In the fall of 1963 this committee of three submitted a report on the radio and television situation in Canada. I further understand that on the basis of the report of this committee it was decided that applications for new and alternative television services could not be approved until July 1, 1964.
That was the first freeze. Why this freeze was made, I do not quite know. It is interesting, however, and I do not want to say anything further on this matter except to note that the Members from the constituencies which these channels would serve are all on the Official Opposition side of the House.
The present Advisory Committee on Broadcasting was set up on July 6, 1964;

then the whole question went into a really deep freeze and we are told that we must wait until the committee finishes its deliberations -this is supposed to be accomplished by next month-at which time a report would be produced. This is all very interesting, Mr. Speaker, but I think there are many questions that still could be asked about this matter. I mention it because the people of Saskatoon are at the present time busy signing a big petition to present to the Minister responsible for reporting to Parliament for the C.B.C., and I believe they are quite responsible in this kind of attitude. Mr. Speaker, I would like to use the time I have available in this debate for two purposes; the first to make some general observations about the budget, and the second to deal in rather more detail with the economic and human problems arising out of the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
In a general discussion of the Budget, I must say on behalf of my constituents that they are plainly very disappointed. Everyone tries to give epithets to a budget, and I would say that this one is very much a status quo budget. Last year's budget was a stand pat budget; and I am afraid I shall run out of synonyms for conservative-with a small "c"-no change budgets if the Minister continues to produce this type of budget. Because it is our contention, Mr. Speaker, that a budget can be used as the instrument of social justice, it can be used as the instrument of economic planning; and I find neither of these in this particular Budget.
In my riding most of the people are workers in industry, and I would say that a fair average wage would be $5,000 a year. Many of the people in my riding are old age pensioners trying to eke out an existence on a pension of $75 a month. I would think that if we are to have-and we have to welcome it-a measure of relaxation from taxes, that relaxation ought to be applied to those who most need it. If we are to have social justice in this country it means a greater degree of equality; it means helping those who are in difficulties. It seems to me ludicrous to be talking in the Speech from the Throne about wars on poverty, and then a little later producing a budget the effect of which is to give an added income of $6,000 a year to those-
The Budget-Mr. Brewin

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I am sorry; my tongue slipped for a moment, and I did not mean to arouse the Minister from his present relaxation. I meant, of course, to say $600. I do not believe a person with an income of $30,000 needs an extra $600 at the present time. I think most of those fortunate enough to be in that bracket would continue to be willing to pay the taxes needed to effect social justice and carry out a war on poverty. I am quite certain that the people in my constituency would rather forgo the $30 a year they are supposed to be saving in order to see that the older people in their midst do at least receive $100 a month.
I have had many, many letters, as has, I am sure, the Minister and I imagine all other hon. Members, before the Budget came out urging that if there were to be tax reductions they should take the form of relieving those at the lower end of the income scale from the necessity of paying income taxes at all by means of raising the exemptions. I have also had letters, as I imagine has every other hon. Member of the House, saying how extraordinarily difficult it is to ask older people to live on $75 a month. If we are to use the Budget as an instrument of social justice, then this is what we should be doing. That is why I say my constituents will be disappointed in this particular Budget.
This Budget does not have an expansionary or growth effect, as I see it. If one takes the situation, as one must, in light of the immediate economic effects of the Canada Pension Plan, the net result is that in the year 1966 most of the people in a constituency like mine will in fact have less money to spend on the necessities of life and on looking after their families. I illustrate that by pointing out that if we take the average taxpayer in my riding who is earning $5,000 a year by way of salary or wage, in 1965 he will pay $15 less in income tax. In the year 1966 he will pay $30 less. But in the year 1966 he will be obliged to pay, or it will be paid for him out of his wage or salary, $79.20 to the Canada Pension Plan fund, quite apart altogether from what his employer has to pay; and as we all know, no benefits become payable until 1967.
I do not mean for one moment to suggest that we do not welcome the Canada Pension Plan; and it is, of course, necessary in a contributory plan to start paying contributions before you can begin to receive benefits. But

April 30, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Brewin the adjustment of income tax should be directed toward seeing that in the lower income brackets the effect of the Canada Pension Plan does not bring about a reduction in the purchasing power of the average worker. Of course if my constituent who is earning $5,000 a year happened to be a self-employed storekeeper he would have to pay $158.40 to the Canada Pension Plan; therefore his saving by way of income tax over the two years would be more than eaten up and would be very much exceeded by his payments to the Plan. So the net result of the operation will be less income in the pocket of the ordinary person for consumption purposes than was the case before.
I think this state of affairs is a thoroughly traditionally-minded approach on the part of this Government, which is trying to justify a tax reduction of $600 for those with incomes of $30,000 while conferring on those of small or modest means minute benefits. In fact, some receive no benefits at all. This does not correspond, as I understand it, with the advice of the Economic Council, which urged the necessity for maintaining purchasing power as an anti-deflationary method of maintaining a high level of demand and employment. The Minister of Finance must be quite satisfied, from the form of his Budget, that no sort of expansion was necessary. He took comfort, as we all do, from the fact that there is a reduced rate of unemployment, the figure now being 3.9 per cent or nearly 4 per cent of the working force. But that is not a satisfactory level of employment, and it seems to me that we should continue to buttress demand by giving tax reductions to the people who need them the most and who would spend the money the quickest.
The most retrogressive step in the Budget is one which no doubt will be hailed with the greatest enthusiasm by supporters of the Government. This is the proposal to create a Canada Development Corporation. We in this party have believed in the necessity for a Canada Development Corporation. We believe we can provide for and expand economic growth by a publicly owned, publicly directed marshalling of investment funds and their integration into an over-all plan for the growth and expansion of the Canadian economy.
What the Minister of Finance has proposed, as I understand it, is a very different thing. A Corporation will be set up by a contribution of $100 million from public funds; the borrowing of another $100 million, perhaps

from public funds; the transfer of the highly successful, publicly owned Polymer Corporation to the new corporation; and the raising of the balance by various means, including insurance companies, trust companies, state trusts, individuals, and I think provincial governments were mentioned. As I understand it a limit is to be imposed on contributions by any one individual or body. The limitation is to be 3 per cent of the total capital involved, which is to be $1 billion, or a limitation of $30 million.
I am sure not too many Canadians or companies other than large corporations will have $30 million to invest. This corporation is not to be publicly owned or publicly directed. Its policies will not be integrated in an over-all economic plan controlled by the Government, but in a short time I suggest it will be controlled by the larger shareholders. Anyone who is aware of the economic facts of life knows that you do not need a majority of shares to control a corporation. If the various insurance companies and other financial institutions each subscribing 3 per cent get together in some sort of mutual trust or arrangement there is not the slightest doubt that they will be able to control the people who will be the majority directors.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
The Minister of Finance thinks there is something magic about having a minority of directors on some boards, and that was evidenced in the legislation he produced previously; but a minority holding is not a great deal of help if the investments of these people are controlled by financial organizations.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is typical of this present Liberal administration. It starts out with an announcement about Liberal and Progressive policies, most of which it has borrowed from the Party of which I am a member. We have talked about Canada Development Corporation for years. The Minister has borrowed the name, but the actuality is something different. I know he will feel that he is being attacked from both sides, because I notice the financial press is beginning to criticize him on the ground that this is a socialistic experiment. It is nothing of the sort.

That gentleman is both a personal and professional friend of mine, but when I want to ascertain things about financial policies I do not consult Mr. Donald Fleming. I assure the Minister that I would be very happy to protect him from the accusation of Mr. Fleming that he is bringing in some sort of socialistic institution. It is far from that. I suggest to the Minister that if we are going to have a Canadian Development Corporation it should be in such a form that the public will have control, so the policies of this Corporation can be part of an economic plan for the benefit and expansion of Canada as a whole, consistent with the advice that should be given to the Government by the Economic Council and other instruments of economic planning and advice. If we do not do that we will get something which in name is a Canada Development Corporation but in fact is another superfluous institution.
I indicated that I intended to deal with the automobile agreement made between Canada and the United States which was announced on January 10 by the Minister of Industry. We in this Party, and I believe a great many people outside as well, believe this agreement is generally sound. It does hold out the hope that eventually there will be an expansion of Canadian markets. It does provide for the integration of this industry, and we hope and believe that in this movement toward more free trade we will be putting the Canadian industry on a sounder basis. However, we know this is only an experiment and that other action along this line may be expected in respect of other matters.
There are a number of matters connected with this automobile agreement which are of tremendous importance because, as I say, this is a change in the whole trade pattern of Canada. We are, however, disquieted by a number of things. This action was taken by Order in Council, I presume under the auspices of the Tariff Act rather than
The Budget-Mr. Brewin by legislation, so we have not had an opportunity in this House of discussing the details of this plan or of having them explained to us.
There are two specific features of this agreement which we find extremely disquieting. One is the fact that we are told that eventually, after a long term, the Canadian consumer may receive the benefit of reduced prices for automobiles. At the present moment the effect of the plan will be to give a bonus of roughly $50 million in reduced duties to the three main Canadian automobile corporations which, as everyone knows, are subsidiaries of United States companies. This reduction is not being passed on, and the Government in making this agreement with the automobile manufacturers does not seem to have sought to exact any term which would require the passing on of this $50 million in reduced prices to the Canadian consumer. Prices have remained exactly the same. The expectation of reduced prices has not been realized and may not be realized for many years.
I understand that the spokesmen for these automobile companies have claimed that they need the $50 million for internal expansion. These companies do not make public their profit figures, I understand, but I have every reason to believe that their profits are considerable and that these are large and well to do corporations, perfectly able to finance their expansions without, as it were, a bonus of $50 million.
I suggest that when future plans of this sort are evolved part of the structure must be in the form of an undertaking by the manufacturers who are to benefit to pass on that benefit in reduced prices to the consumers. It has been suggested that increased competition may bring this about, but who seriously believes there is effective competition in respect of the prices of automobiles among the very few companies which are in this field? We know these companies live in a regime of managed prices. I suggest that when the Government of this country enters into agreements of this sort with other countries for the benefit of manufacturers in this country-and it is merely incidental that they are subsidiaries of United States companies-it should exact as part of the agreements undertakings that the benefits will be passed on to Canadian consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with the disquieting factors arising out of the United States-Canada automobile agreement and I had dealt with one, namely the failure to pass on the benefits of reduced costs to the consumer. I now want to pass on to the second disquieting factor, the failure of the Government to make clearcut, adequate and timely provision for the individuals dislocated or affected by the adjustments to be made as the result of the agreement. It would, I suggest, be most unfair and it would be an effective deterrent to the working out of more agreements of this sort in the future if the burden of the adjustment were to fall on individual employees and their families.
I have already pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that it is estimated that some $50 million will be saved by the three major companies involved by way of reduction in the duties that they are required to pay. Canadian consumers can also hope to benefit in the future. But it would be totally wrong if the benefits that are going to the companies now and the benefits that we hope will be passed on to the consumers later were to be achieved at the expense of serious economic loss and the loss of jobs by those in the industry. I suggest, therefore, that the Government has a duty to ensure that individuals in the Canadian automobile industry directly affected should not suffer economic loss as a result of the agreement.
I want to make a contrast, which does no credit to the Government I think, between the situation in the United States, the other partner to the agreement, and the situation in Canada. Under the American legislation, which is being discussed at the present moment in Congress, there is detailed provision for the protection of those who are affected.
I urge that Canadian workers are entitled to protection at least as definite and at least as generous as that being accorded to American workers in the same position. I have here the American legislation, which I do not have time to go into in detail. The Bill is H.R. 6960 and Title 3 deals in detail with what is called adjustment assistance. I might summarize some of the effects of this adjustment assistance. It supplements the benefits payable under the United States Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and proposes liberal guidelines for the granting of adjustment assistance benefits over and above those provided for in the 
DEBATES	April 30, 1965
Trade Expansion Act. Adjustment assistance benefits will be the equivalent of 65 per cent of the individual worker's average weekly wage or 65 per cent of the national manufacturing average weekly wage, whichever is less. Excluded from these benefits, which is a very important point in working them out, are the supplementary insurance benefits payable under the collective agreements within the industry itself.
The .Canadian situation has been very different. The United Automobile Workers have been seeking for months to find out from the Government just what action was proposed. The prospective lay-offs have been anticipated for a matter of months but it has not been possible to find any equivalent action. I presume one of the reasons for this is that action in Canada has been taken by Order in Council and not by legislation. I suggest that we need legislation spelling out the assistance to which dislocated workers are entitled which is just as clearcut as the American legislation.
I know that even yesterday a deputation from the United Automobile Workers' Union called upon Members of the Government and spoke to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen), the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), I believe, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), who naturally has a special interest in this matter. But it is just not good enough to have the sort of vague announcement that the Minister of Industry gave us today in answer to a question from the hon. Member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis). All he said was that the Department of Labour is going to mobilize its efforts, and we are told that some formula is going to be worked out. My suggestion is that we need action on this matter at once. The industry needs it, the people of Canada need it and so does Parliament because this is a very important problem. If the program of developing trade on a continent-wide basis is to be expanded, we must be sure that the result of this first experiment is not dissatisfaction, dislocation and hardship to individual workers.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
We know already, and we were told today, that the first big lay-off at the Ford Motor Company of Canada has been reduced, perhaps as a result of discussions, to some 49. However, in the course of this year this one plant will probably lay off 1,500 people. They may be able to obtain other employment, and I hope they will. The Minister was optimistic about this. I suggest we need something to

The automobile workers are in favour of the general principle of this particular agreement. However, the Vice President of this very large organization had this to say, according to a report:
He also decried the failure of the Canadian Government thus far to provide protection for Canadian workers and their families similar to that proposed in the United States and he scored auto manufacturers for failing to pass on to consumers in Canada the $50 million a year savings they are realizing as a result of the removal of the Canadian tariff.

Commenting on the failure of the Canadian Government to provide protection for Canadian workers displaced by reason of the new agreement, Woodcock called on the Johnson administration to make known to the Canadian Government the concern of the United States that adequate safeguards be provided for the Canadian workers affected by the agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I begin these remarks by extending my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) for the budget message he delivered to us the other day, a message he delivered with such grace and eloquence, and I congratulate him most of all because of the demonstration that he gave us on that occasion of his qualifications for the post that he occupies and of his successful stewardship over our national finances.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say these things because I recall only too vividly the abuse that was showered on my hon. colleague some two years ago in the House. On that occasion I had the privilege of helping to defend him against the very unfair attacks made upon him. I believed then, as I believe now, that Canada has never had a more dedicated or a more competent Minister of Finance.
When the Minister of Finance took over the management of our finances they were in a state of disorder and confusion. There had not been an adequate accounting for a couple of years, as is better known to those who were Members of the House at that time than it was to me; but I heard something about it from the outside, and I remember only too well, since I was engaged in an election campaign against a former minister of finance, how much the disorder and confusion of those days told against the government then in office.
Not only were the finances of our country in a state of confusion when this Government and my colleague took over, but there was even greater confusion and uncertainty throughout the country, as I can testify since I was one of those who, at that particular time, did not have the privilege of sitting in this House and had to judge events from the outside. The greatest tribute that I can pay to my colleague this afternoon is to say that our finances are in order and confidence has been restored.
Perhaps the best evidence that I can present on this subject was produced for me yesterday by the hon. Member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Hamilton) who gave a most extraordinary speech in the House in which, in effect, he said that his Government did not have control over policies in the financial field. He admitted this. One has only to read the speech to recognize the fact that he knew, even though he seemed to have been
The Budget-Mr. Sharp unable to persuade his colleagues, that the monetary policy of the country was out of the control of the Government.
The hon. Member for Qu'Appelle in the course of his speech yesterday also spoke about how the star of my hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance, was rising. I am sorry the hon. Member is not here today but I can only say to him and other hon. gentlemen that nothing delights me more. It may be that in making these remarks the hon. Member for Qu'Appelle was thinking about his own Party when trying to drive a wedge between the Minister of Finance and me, but I can assure you that we rejoice in one another's successes and we share in one another's misfortunes. So far as we on this side of the House are concerned, when the star of the Minister of Finance is in the ascendancy the Government is in the ascendancy, and we all know this.
Just about a year ago during the budget debate, the hon. Member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), as reported in Hansard for March 16, 1964, at page 996, said in reference to the claims of the Minister of Finance that he was working toward a balanced budget at a high level of employment:
If that, Mr. Speaker, is a step toward a balanced budget, then it is going to be a long, long time before we attain that end.
It did not take a long, long time. It took exactly one fiscal year to reduce the deficit in our national finances to about $80 million which, when we are raising and spending such large sums of money, is the same thing as saying that our accounts were in balance. And when I think back to the years before we had the privilege of the stewardship of the present Minister to the deficits of over $700 million, then I am thankful, and I say it once again with the greatest confidence, that we have the present Minister in his present job.
But, Mr. Speaker, a balanced budget is not the only purpose or even the main purpose of Government financial policy, and in this respect I agree with the remarks made yesterday by the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cow-ichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron), and so, I know, does the Minister of Finance. The aim of this Government is and has been to balance the budget at a high level of economic activity, and we have succeeded. Not only do we have these purposes and these policies, we achieve them.



April 30, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Sharp
I admit, as the hon. Member has said, that a balanced budget is by no means the main purpose of Government financial policy; nor is a chronic deficit. I get the impression from listening to my hon. friend and some of his colleagues on that side that they look upon a chronic deficit as the supreme financial virtue. I have listened very carefully to their speeches because the New Democratic Party always gives me the impression of being the party with a halo around its head, as having invented all the good things, and being the only Party in the House that is opposed to sin.
I am never very much persuaded by what I hear, but one thing does impress me; that is,
I do not think they realize that it is important for the attainment of high employment, that it is important for the elimination of unemployment, that the people of this country and of the world as a whole have confidence in the financial integrity and stability of Canada.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
One of the reasons my hon. friends do not make the impact upon the country that they would like to make is that the public believes they do not understand that. Now, Mr. Speaker, when one looks at the economy of the country as distinct from its national finances, the contrast with conditions two years ago is even more striking. We are undoubtedly experiencing one of the great periods of expansion and certainly one of the most prolonged in the history of the country. I do not say by any means that this is due only or primarily to the policies .of the Government. What I do assert with confidence is that the policies followed by this Government have helped, and helped .substantially, to achieve the results that have been achieved. One of the best evidences of this is that although we are, of course, as we always are, influenced greatly by conditions abroad, and particularly in the United States, our economic record surpasses that of the United States.
I give some of the credit for this to the policies of my colleague the Minister of Finance and of the Government as a whole. When I say this, Mr. Speaker, I think about some of the complaints from the Opposition, that our policies were going to damage the economy; that they were going to bring the expansion to a halt. Indeed, on every occasion that I have heard any speaker from the other side speak in a budget debate, they have said, "The Government is not following the right policies. They are going to bring this expansion to a halt. They are very fortu-

nate; they have horseshoes around their necks; they have four-leaf clovers in their hands. It is not due to anything the Government is doing; it is just good fortune. The policies they are following are wrong. The country is prospering notwithstanding the stupidity of the Government". This is the kind of argument I have heard over these last two years.
I would like, by way of answer, to point to the record, and the best record I can point to in this respect is that of the investment intentions, plans and expenditures of Canadian businessmen. If in fact the policies of this Government had been of such a character as has been charged by the Members of the Opposition, that would have been reflected in the actions of Canadian businessmen. I remember in particular the moans from the other side of the House about the effect of our policies, particularly our taxation policies, upon business investment in new plant and equipment. It began two years ago; the complaint was made that businessmen were going to be discouraged. Were they discouraged?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they were.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

At the beginning of 1964, by way of answer to this charge-which is again being repeated-I tabled the first estimate of investment intentions for the year 1964. I tabled that report with some satisfaction because it showed an increase of approximately 8 per cent in investment intentions of Canadian business. In spite of what the Opposition characterized as the discouraging policies, or the detrimental policies, of this Government I was able to report to the House, at the middle of the year 1964, after we had made another survey of the intentions of Canadian businessmen and of their expenditures, that expenditures in 1964 were going to be, not 8 per cent better than 1963 but 16 per cent better. This is the kind of discouragement we were giving to Canadian business. I heard my hon. friends say at that time that this was only the effect of the sales tax, that the businessman was trying to get ahead of the increase in the sales tax. But when we did the survey again at the beginning of 1965, it showed that businessmen intended to invest another 14 per cent or 15 per cent over and above what they had invested in 1964. If this is discouragement, it is the kind of discouragement that I think we would all like to see. A 30 per cent increase in the level of business expenditures for new plant and equipment, in two years-that is the result of the policies being followed by this Government.

May I say a word more about exports.
I have talked about the 19 per cent increase, and as Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board I quite freely acknowledge that a very large part of the increase in exports last year was due to wheat sales. I know that my hon. frends opposite who represent the prairie provinces are happy that that was so, but even if we eliminate wheat the increase in the export of other goods was 17 per cent, which was the largest year to year increase in exports in our history.
While speaking of wheat may I say this. Although in the present crop year we are not going to attain the very remarkable alltime record of last year, this will probably be the second largest crop year for exports of wheat and flour in our history. Moreover, I have fixed a target and announced it, so that everyone can look at it. Our objective for this crop year and the two following years is 1,200 million bushels of wheat and flour, which is more than has ever been exported in any three-year period. When I hear hon. Members opposite say that we do not have objectives for the expansion of Canadian trade, I can put forward that figure as a prime example of our courage and enterprise.
The most important aspect of the increase in exports last year was the continuing increase in the export of manufactured goods. I say this because it has been alleged that the policies we have been following have not been sufficiently expansive in this direction. I have acknowledged, and I acknowledge again, the initiative taken by the previous Government. They took some very useful initiatives in expanding trade. I have always considered, and I do now, that this is an area in which there is precious little room for partisanship. It is an enterprise in which we all have such great stakes and we should join in the efforts that are being made. However, I do want to point out that the increase in exports of manufacturing goods has been nearly 100 per cent in the last three years. That is, the increase in the export of end products, all types of machinery, equipment, finished consumer goods, which rose by one third last year, has increased by nearly 100 per cent over the last three years. May I also add a word about our trade with Britain which, for some reason I find difficult to understand, has not been commented upon by any of the speakers who have participated in this debate. When this Government took office in April 1963 we found the British people and the British government extremely disheartened about their trade with Canada. I took advantage at the earliest opportunity of going to London to discover the reasons and to try and remove the psychological block that seemed to exist in relations between Britain and Canada with respect to trade. My colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) made a trip as well for the same purpose, and we found out the reasons the British were so disheartened. May I recall what they were.
First of all, they were very disheartened by the memories of the attitude of the previous government to Britain's application to join the European Common Market. This seems to have had a peculiar effect upon the British, who felt that somehow Canada was no longer interested in the welfare of the British people and would be willing to stand in the way of what they considered a constructive move.

House for debate at this time is an amendment to the motion that the Speaker leave the Chair, constituting a want of confidence motion based on such things as the removal of the sales tax on building materials and so on. It is well to remind ourselves that these phony no confidence motions are simply no confidence motions, regardless of what may be the wording that follows; in other words, they are very simply an expression by this House, should they carry, of no confidence in the present administration, and all the reasons that may be spelled out in the wording of the motion have no effect whatever.
Mr. Speaker, you and all other hon. Members of this House know full well that if this motion is carried-in fact if it were carried unanimously- by the Members of this House, it would not have the effect of reducing the sales tax on building materials. The only effect that could come from supporting the motion now before the House would be the requirement that the Government resign, that this Parliament dissolve, and that we have an election. That is what we have to decide when we vote one way or the other on this motion.
The Canadian Press, who are usually very fair and objective in their reporting of the proceedings in this House, had this to say in an article datelined Ottawa which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of today, April 30:
Social Credit Leader Thompson and his three western followers voted against the increase in exemptions and the old age pension rates-
That is a complete and absolute misrepresentation of the facts, Mr. Speaker, and to prove that point-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I see there is some mumbling over here in the Tory Party. There were a number of times between 1958 and 1962 when ever;/ one of the 208 Members that were present-and most of the time they were not all here-voted against this kind of no confidence motion; against one that called for an increase in family allowances, for example. They voted repeatedly against this kind of motion that called for changes in the income tax structure.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals even voted for debt free money on one of these phony motions in 1962.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So debt free money is phony, is it?

April 30, 1965

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All I am trying to do is establish the fact that these motions are ones to dissolve Parliament, and nothing else. When they are reported in the press and they single out certain Members as being against increases in the basic exemption for income tax and raises in the rates of old age security pensions, that is a gross misrepresentation of the facts. I think we have long passed the date when we ought to have some changes in the rules of procedure in this House so that we do not need to perpetuate this kind of deception. There are a number of cases in the past, and every single Party-particularly the two Parties which have had the responsibility of administration-has been put in the position of apparently voting against something that is desirable. Those of us in this House and in the Press Gallery and other places should understand the effect of supporting this kind of motion, and should know exactly what they are for, and it is not what has been reported in the press during the last few hours.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought you were going to bolster up the Government when you started your speech.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
