maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to talk about the provisions of the budget in that important sector of our economy, namely agriculture. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), as reported at page 428 of Hansard, said in his speech on Monday night:
All areas of the country, almost all types of industry and agriculture, and most groups in the community are sharing in this advance.
Of course he is referring to the current situation, and the outlook, as far as the economy is concerned.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I have some reports before me published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. One of them was published in March 1965, and in the section dealing with the net income 22620-521
The Budget-Mr. Olson of farm operators from farming operations between the years 1962 to 1964 it indicates that the net income to farmers for all Canada in 1962 stood at $1,627 million. By 1963 this figure had gone up to $1,654 million; in other words, a slight increase of some $27 million in the net income of farmers in the country. During 1964, Mr. Speaker, it slipped to $1,432 million, or went down over $200 million.
If what the Minister of Finance has said in this budget speech is true, and if that is his opinion and he has facts and figures to back up his statement that agriculture has shared in the advances of the economy in 1964, then I would suggest to him that he tell the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to quit publishing false reports. Because if net farm income went down by $200 million between 1963 and 1964, surely those farmers have not participated in the expansion of the economy. It does not take a great economist to realize that it is the net income that matters.
Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made a comment on this question. The hon. Member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), following on what the Minister of Finance had to say, asked, as reported at page 428 of Hansard:
Is that why the farmers are coming to Ottawa on Wednesday?
And the Prime Minister interjected:
To get even more.
To get even more decline in their net income; is that what the Prime Minister meant? Because the Dominion Bureau of Statistics indicates that that is what is happening. It also suggests that if there was not something very seriously wrong with the net income position of farmers in Canada today we would not have had the kind of demonstration which we did have on Parliament Hill last Wednesday. Farmers are generally not prone to making displays such as this, unless they are severely provoked into so doing. At the moment I prefer to accept the figures published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, which indicate there has been a substantial decline in the net income of farmers, rather than the opinion expressed by the Minister of Finance that agriculture too has shared in the growth of the economy.
Another publication was issued, Mr. Speaker, by the Department of Agriculture in August 1964 entitled "The Economic Annalist". On page 74 the following appears, and I will refer directly to it so there is no misinterpretation of what the index figures

April 30, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Olson stand for. According to this the prices of commodities and services used by farmers, the things required by farmers which go into their cost of operation, based on an index figure of 100 for the period 1935 to 1939, went up to an index point of 309.9 in April 1964. There are other figures to indicate what is the index figure for the commodities they sell, and at the same period they had reached a composite figure of 245.8. Therefore the difference between the cost of operation and the prices received by the primary producers of food and groceries, as the Minister of Agriculture prefers to call them, indicates a 65 point lag since 1939. I think it is highly unfair and unjust, Mr. Speaker, for the Minister of Finance to suggest that the agricultural sector of the Canadian economy has shared in the expansion of the whole of the Canadian economy.
In the budget papers attached as an appendix to Hansard on Monday last there appears at page 145 a table showing the total appropriation out of the federal treasury for the Department of Agriculture for the year ending March 31, 1961, namely the amount of $194.5 million. For the year ending March 1962 the figure had gone up to $218.7 million. In 1963 it had slipped back to $183.4 million; and for the year ending March 31, 1964 it had gone up again to $225.7 million. The estimated expenditure for this past year is down to $168 million. Many hon. Members have referred to this same matter in this budget debate. If the Dominion Bureau of Statistics is correct in suggesting that there has been a decline of $200 million in the net income of all farmers in Canada, it seems to me that it is the wrong time for the Minister of Agriculture and the Government of the day to be appropriating less money to this important, in fact basic, sector of our whole economy. It is rather disturbing, Mr. Speaker, to note that the $168 million appropriated is to cover all expenditures to support management, research and everything else for agriculture, and at the same time there is a requirement of well over $1 billion by way of interest on the national debt.
This net income problem for agriculture generally has reached a crisis. In Western Canada it has not been felt quite as severely lately because of a certain sell-off of inventory. There was an accumulation of large quantities of wheat during the 1950's and there was an enormous sell-off of this wheat in 1961, continuing into 1962, 1963 and 1964. I suggest that when this inventory has been sold and the farmers return to an income level based on current production the effects are going to be felt in Western Canada, even though the pain has not yet arrived. However, the crisis already exists in most parts of Eastern Canada.
While the Minister of Agriculture announced some change in dairy policy which may be beneficial, provided it is pursued vigorously and more effort and money is put into it, I suggest that this crisis has reached the position where we need some kind of immediate action to tide us over the intervening period. Following that we need to work out a whole new agricultural policy for Canada which will not only stop this decline in the net income but bring about an increase once more from year to year.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Not many days ago, Mr. Speaker, I said in this House that we will give the Conservatives full marks for all the policies they brought in which were beneficial and useful to farmers generally. We will give the Liberals full marks for all the policies they brought in, such as increasing the availability of farm credit through the farm improvement loans legislation, and so on. None of these policies has done anything to come to grips with the cost-price squeeze that has been taking place.
The cost of production has been accelerating, yet the prices the farmers receive for their produce have been, if only slightly, declining. This problem requires long-range programming. Surely the time has come when we should stop worrying about which Party receives the credit for accomplishing certain things. There are some men in all Parties of this House who I am sure could make valuable contributions to the development of policies and programs which would reverse this trend. I hope there will be a determined and concerted effort to work out policies of this kind in order to provide farmers with positive results, without too much concern about which Party should receive credit.
The Minister of Finance also mentioned in his budget speech, as well as in answer to a question today, that the cost of land clearing and draining would be allowable as a write-off from income in the current year, to the extent of 100 per cent. I have had a great deal of experience in this regard and I appreciate the Minister's statement to that effect. I should like to ask the Minister a specific question in relation to a related expense. Will the cost of land levelling in irrigation districts in Canada, such as Southern Alberta, be allowable as write-offs from expenses in

April 30. 1965



current years? The Minister will appreciate that the levelling of land is important to a successful irrigation project. In the past these expenses have not been allowed as write-offs in current years. There was some suggestion that these expenses should be added to the value of the land but, of course, land does not depreciate, so there is no capital cost allowance in this regard. I hope the Minister will take this into consideration and allow these costs to be deducted in the same way that the costs of draining and clearing land are to be allowed.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those are legitimate expenses for increased production.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right. We are somewhat disturbed that there is no provision in the budget for the removal of the discriminatory corporation tax on private power companies. Mr. Smallwood said yesterday that the budget is neither the place nor the time to make this particular announcement. I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) today, because I know he is very close to the Premier of Newfoundland, whether there was some other place or time more appropriate for announcing that this corporation tax on private power companies is to be removed. He replied that this had nothing to do with his Department and that he did not see why he should be expected to answer the question. I thought, in view of the fact the Premier of Newfoundland had made that statement, that the Minister of Transport would know when and where it would be appropriate to make such an announcement. I can think of no more appropriate time for such an announced removal of corporation tax than during the Budget speech. I hope I am not being overly suspicious, but perhaps there is a more politically appropriate time to announce such a removal of tax. If that is what the Premier of Newfoundland had in mind, surely the Minister of Finance should indicate to this House, perhaps not today, when and where that announcement will be made.
Several years ago the Premier of British Columbia called a special session of the Legislature, after the former Government decided not to remove this tax, with a view to expropriating the power companies in that Province. It is my hope that this present Government is not attempting by its policy in this regard to force those Provinces which have not expropriated these private power companies to take over those companies.
It can be proved with solid, sound and almost indisputable fact that the private
The Budget-Mr. Olson power companies in the Province of Alberta, operating similar sized plants with the same kind of fuel as those operating in the Province of Saskatchewan, can produce power much more cheaply than can be produced in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why do you not tell Mr. Bennett that?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why did you not tell Mr. Bennett and the Minister of Finance that you intended to remove this discriminatory tax during the time when you were in power, with 208 Members?
Federal Governments, both past and present, have stubbornly refused to treat these power companies in Alberta and in Newfoundland on the same basis as the power companies in the rest of Canada are treated. Publicly owned power corporations are not subject to this same tax. Calgary Power and several of the other private power companies in Alberta have given a firm undertaking to pass on any savings resulting from the removal of this tax, to which they are subjected, to the consumers through lower power rates. There is no provision for the removal of this tax in the Budget speech.
There are one or two other subjects which I should like to mention. There is no provision in the Budget speech for adjustments to the 11 per cent sales tax on materials in masonry walls. The brick tile and ceramic industry in Canada has been discriminated against very severely by reason of the fact that there is an exemption from sales tax on poured concrete in walls, except for the cement content, which is a very small part of the total cost. There is also an exemption from sales tax on concrete bricks used in the construction of walls. On the other hand, the full tax applies to bricks and other ceramic tiles, including raw materials, labour and transportation, used for the construction of walls. Surely this is an injustice. The method of calculating the tax on materials used for this type of construction should be the same, regardless of the materials used. I hope the Minister will give some consideration to this situation.
I should now like to refer to our national accounts. At page 428 of Hansard the Minister stated:
If the accounts are translated into a form more suitable for measuring their impact on the economy, that is, into terms of the national economic accounts, the change in two years is from a deficit of $399 million in 1962-63 to a surplus of $332 million in the last fiscal year-an improvement of over $700 million.

April 30, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Olson [DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We need some explanation of what he is talking about when he speaks about national economic accounts. If you look at the papers that we filed you find that we have an $83 million deficit. In addition, we find on page 137 of the appendices that the increase in the net debt during the fiscal year was $479.4 million. Dirt farmers like the hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and myself, Mr. Speaker, do not understand how you can have a $399 million surplus and at the same time add $479 million to the national debt. Then we have another figure which shows an $83 million deficit.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend would permit a question from another sometime dirt farmer. Have the explanations that were given in the Budget White Papers and in the Report of the Bank of Canada as to the difference in these accounting methods come to his attention?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have all the papers before me, Mr. Speaker, the Budget White Papers and the Report of the Bank of Canada for the year 1934. I want to say to the Minister that I have read all of them very carefully but I do not understand it all. That may be my problem, but I wonder whether the Minister and all the officials of his Department and the Bank of Canada agree on these figures and on the formula of arriving at these certain positions of surplus and deficit all over the place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they do.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder whether they do. We would like to have some understanding of these things. The Minister of Finance prefers to use the national economic accounts. Do they take into account total productivity? Are they something similar to the gross national product, with certain adjustments being made for intergovernment transfers and so on? Is this an adjustment that has been made in Canada's relationship with regard to other countries? It is all rather confusing, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to use different bases to calculate what the end result is going to be. As a dirt farmer I am interested in the results.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is more complicated than dirt farming.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is another point. There is an increase in the national debt of $479.4 million. I should like to ask the Minister this question. Is this figure before adding on the

$396 million transferred from what he called the actuarial deficit in the superannuation fund, or is it the case that during these past few weeks we have added $800 million rather than $400 million to the net national debt? There was an item in the supplementary estimates that provided for the transfer of this so-called actuarial deficit to the national debt of Canada and I want to know whether we are that much more in debt in addition to the $479 million.
There is another point on which I should like information. What about the interest that was paid? I hope I am getting these terms right, but was this actuarial deficit of $396 million with interest or without interest when this deficit was being carried in the superannuation account? If it was without interest, then the Canadian people have been paying something like $20 million a year in interest charges that have not been reported. I am not blaming the present Minister of Finance because I know that this practice has been going on for a long time and that the former government was covering up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. Member as his time has expired. Has he unanimous consent to continue beyond his time?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much. I want to express my appreciation to the House for this consideration. To get back to the argument, I should like to know whether this $396 million was with or without interest. I should also like the Minister of Finance to answer this question. When the former Government was in office and this actuarial deficit was building up, was there not an obligation on the part of the Government of the day to make these transfers as required, and was the practice followed not simply a bookkeeping way of covering up an additional deficit that they should have shown? In other words, the large deficits that did occur every year while the former Government was in office were not being accurately reported through the estimates and through the Budget.
I am not going to abuse the privilege granted by the House of speaking beyond my time. I seriously question the wisdom of bringing in tax cuts and budgeting for a deficit at the same time. I say that because the interest charges on our national debt have now reached almost $1,100 million. If we relate this figure to other expenditures we
April 30, 1S6S

will find that the interest is now twice as much as all the family allowances paid for all of the children in Canada. It is about 50 per cent more than all the old age pensions paid to all of the senior citizens of Canada. When you think in those terms, Mr. Speaker, it is evident that it is a great deal of money.
This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) brought up a very interesting point. He said that maybe the deficit of $300 million being budgeted for will not materialize. Have we not reached the point, Mr. Speaker, where we can have the expenditure and revenue estimates placed before the House, after being calculated as accurately as possible? Is the Minister of Finance attempting to budget for a deficit of $300 million when he really and honestly believes it will not be that high? As a matter of fact, the former minister of finance, the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), suggested that the interest charges on the national debt shown in the blue book are deliberately changed. In other words, they are deliberately expressed in such a way that people are unable to anticipate what is in the Budget. I make a plea to the Minister of Finance that all the figures in the estimates and in the budget be calculated on the most accurate basis possible within the limits imposed by trying to estimate before they are brought before the House.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that while there are probably some beneficial provisions in the budget we think that the matter of the discriminatory tax on private power corporations, the collecting of taxes on masonry walls and other things that were not dealt with should also be taken into account by the Minister of Finance, and that he should at least try to do justice so that Government taxation does not upset the competitive balance between the various sectors of our economy.

Mr. Speaker, one can hardly imagine the difficulties I have encountered in order to deliver my speech. Yesterday, members spoke for an hour at least so as to prevent me from speaking and today, thanks to the generosity of the ministers and other members, those who had the floor before me spoke so long that there are barely 20 minutes left at my disposal. Nevertheless, I shall begin with the remarks 1 was to make at the end of my speech, for I will probably not have enough time for all
The Budget-Mr. Caron those things I wanted to say, since the discussion on the budget has to be called off at five o'clock, and I am sure the house and the government will not do me the favour of allowing me to continue beyond my time.
Mr. Speaker, for the last two years a special committee has been considering the possibility of shortening the sessions. During that time, many changes were brought about, particularly with respect to committees; for two years we have been sitting continuously and without holidays.
I wonder if that committee did not think for a moment about the possibility of changing human nature. Had it been able to change human nature, we could have avoided prolonged debates and saved time during the sessions. But everything is going on as before, in spite of changes, and I am even wondering if we will be able to enjoy holidays this year. It seems that we will witness long debates. The most academic debates, namely those on the speech from the throne and on the budget, do not fall under that category because they have a limited period; but when we discuss legislative measures, I am convinced that the opposition will bring forth many objections, and in view of this obstruction, I am wondering if we shall not be compelled to call a general election. In my opinion, at the present time, this would be the most practical and most logical step.
Mr. Speaker, changes must be made, and particularly basic changes.
For instance, we could do away with the non-confidence motions. I know that this scares some people who claim that we would thus be drifting away from England where a vote of non-confidence has always existed; however, we must admit that we have closer links with the Americans than with Great Britain, whether we like it or not. In fact, when Mr. Thatcher, the premier of Saskatchewan, was asked what he would do if the province of Quebec seceded from the rest of Canada, he replied: "We would become the 51st American state". This is proof that even the English Canadians feel they are closer to the United States than to England, and therefore I suggest that the non-confidence vote is outdated, as far as Canada is concerned.
That era is long past, and I suggest that we should do away with non-confidence motions. In so doing, we could have a general election at fixed dates, every four or five years, and we would not see these rows at every session, for an election would not

the Greber plan which provided for two stations, one in the north and the other in the south. And it is the southern station that they want to build two miles further away. The northern station would be built in Hull, about two miles from parliament. The management of the Canadian Pacific might have been asked at that time to run their express trains between Ottawa and Montreal from Hull; the service would have been faster because the distance on the north shore is 20 miles shorter.
Nothing of the sort has been granted. Things remained unchanged. They seem to have the impression that there is nothing important on the Hull side; that there is no need to attend to that. Well, I for one claim that the Hull side is important.
The city of Hull was enjoying a special treatment when it was represented by a minister in the cabinet. In fact, the Printing Bureau was built in our city when the hon. Mr. Fournier was minister of Public Works. True, with the assistance of the deputy minister of public works, the Conservatives set themselves to make believe that this building had been erected in a sort of slough, in an area where water was running all day long.
However, Mr. Speaker, I can say this: the finest land in either city had been chosen for the National Printing Bureau. It was a piece of land covered with gravel 17 feet deep and under the gravel the Department of Public Works found rock after boring further into the ground.
It was believed to be rock; huge boulders were struck and it was thought that solid rock had been reached. The layer was determined to be of a certain depth but when the excavating contract was awarded, the contractor found out that the rock consisted only of huge boulders and that further borings would have to be carried out. A contract for excavation to a further depth of 15 feet was awarded but when solid rock was reached, it was found that the foundations would be under the river level and that the water was seeping right through to the site. Consequently, the place was flooded. Means were found to evacuate the water through a city sewer and, today, another underground storey, 15 feet high, could be built if necessary. It would still be possible to evacuate the seeping water. Mr. Speaker, that goes to show that the minister who obtained that project was truly useful to the city.
I did not ask to be appointed to the cabinet. If it was thought that I lacked the required
The Budget-Mr. Caron qualifications, it would have been a simple matter to let me know. I could have resigned so someone could be found who had all the qualifications in the world and had graduated from Laval University or the University of Montreal as an economist. The people of Hull thought I could perform my duties. But if I had been told those things, I would have resigned and made way for somebody better qualified or apparently better qualified to take over the duties of a member of parliament. But enough of that.
I hope that during the year now beginning the department will look toward Hull, because we do not intend to be continually ignored. We plan to insist and insist most strongly, because we are not being refused a favour, but a right. That right we have earned. I am asking for it and will keep asking for it in another session.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is running short and that I will not have time to deal with all the questions I put down.
I find that all members of the opposition always seem to agree on one point, that is bilingualism. Hon. members opposite always agree on one thing, and it is to revolt when mention is made of bilingualism.
Bilingualism is a national reality that cannot be overlooked because it compels recognition in Canada, if confederation is to be maintained. Confederation will not be maintained if bilingualism is not recognized throughout the country.
I have heard members opposite, mostly new Canadians, criticize the action taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), when he proposed the adoption of a flag and when he established the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. They criticized him then but they forgot to say, for instance, that he was the first man in Canada, the first prime minister of Canada who had the courage to choose a new flag and to set up a commission on bilingualism whose members tour Canada to find out what we have the right to expect from Canada.
It must be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that if bilingualism is not recognized within a few years, confederation will be in danger.
The province of Quebec has lost her inferiority complex. The province of Quebec and the French Canadians are beginning to demand what they have a right to expect.
And when I hear criticism from some hon. members, I say to them: You do not know Canadian history, you did not study it properly. I admit that in Quebec and Ontario

April 30, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Caron some history books are not what they should be. But a certain commission is working today to set the record straight as far as Canadian history is concerned.
However, one thing cannot be denied: the Paris treaty of 1763 gives us some guarantees. Mr. Murray, governor in 1760 after the fall of Quebec, also gave the French Canadians what they had the right to have and since then tradition has always given the French Canadians what they had the right to ask for. But things deteriorated until the French Canadian insurrection of 1837. I admit that revolt was a tragedy, a mistake, but lacking arms and money we still showed that we did not intend to let anyone step on our toes.
Since then confederation took place and in 1867 when it became a reality, it was decided to give equal rights to the French Canadians in the spirit of confederation.
But since then, things went wrong in the provinces. It started in New Brunswick and later on the trouble spread to Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba; in short, things went wrong everywhere. Mr. Speaker, in view of those facts, I think that the time has come to give the matter a second thought. If there is no change within the next few years, I will endorse the statement made not too long ago by a Laval University professor who said: "I am no separatist, but if I were convinced that there is a danger of our being submerged and losing our identity in being a part of Canada, I would soon become one".
I therefore ask new Canadians and Canadians of every party in the house to forget the short-lived political gains they may get by fighting French Canadians. Let us unite to get what we are entitled to. I know that if French Canadians in other provinces were, as far as schools are concerned, treated on the same basis as English Canadians in Quebec, in short, if those people had the right to have their own school boards and establish their own curriculum, we would no longer advocate the separation of French and English Canadians, and the constitution would continue to function.
That is why I am asking my friends opposite to think well before making any decisions and to see to it that there is better understanding among the two races of Canada. We could then save confederation and go on for another 100 or 200 years constantly improving the situation, so that all Cana-

dians across Canada might be respected by the various races making up our population. [Text]

speechtext: Is it not the fact that there are some regulations in respect of ocean shipping on the coast that are effected by the Public Utilities Commission; or do they have no jurisdiction whatever?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PUBLIC CARRIERS IN B.C. COASTAL WATERS
speechtext:
The Public Utilities Commission of British Columbia, as far as I am aware, has absolutely no jurisdiction over coastal shipping in British Columbia. The only body that I know of which has any regulatory function is the Canada Steamship Inspection Service, which of course, as I am sure the hon. Member understands, is concerned only with ensuring that the ships which are engaged in travel operate in a manner which is safe, that they carry the necessary life saving apparatus, and that sort of thing.
As I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, section 5 of the Act, which has to do with the matter of the Board of Transport Commissioners dealing with applications for licences, sets out the considerations which the Board may take into consideration in dealing with such applications. I would like to quote part at least of that section. Section 5 (a) says:
Any objection to the application that may be made by any person or persons who are already providing transport facilities, whether by rail or water, on the routes or between the places that the applicant intends to serve, on the ground that suitable facilities are or, if the licence were issued would be in excess of requirements, or on the ground that any of the conditions of any other transport licence held by the applicant have not been complied with;
(b)	whether or not the issue of such licence would tend to develop the complementary rather than the competitive functions of the different forms of transport, if any, involved in such objections;
(c)	the general effect on other transport services and any public interest which may be affected by the issue of such licence; and

April 30, 1965
Transport
(d)	the quality and permanence of the service to be offered by the applicant and his financial responsibility, including adequate provision for the protection of passengers, shippers and the general public by means of insurance.
Mr. Speaker, those are the considerations which, as far as I am aware, generally apply in every other field of transportation in Canada, whether it is by air, bus line- which, for the benefit of the hon. Member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), I would point out comes under the jurisdiction of the Public Utilities Commission of British Columbia- or whether it is by rail. It also applies in certain parts of Canada under the provisions of the Transport Act, but it does not apply between ports or places in British Columbia. [DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Part III of the Act has to do with traffic, tolls and tariffs and contains what I think most people in Canada consider to be the normal provisions with respect to the filing of tariffs, and with opportunity being given to the public being served to register objections and to have their cases heard if they feel that any increases in freight rates or passenger rates are unwarranted. These are the operative provisions of the Transport Act, but as the Act stands these operative provisions have never had any operative effect along the coastal area of British Columbia.
I could recite a long list of the communities of people who have established themselves along the British Columbia coast and who have suffered at times rather extreme hardship owing to the fact that they have had absolutely no court of appeal to decide whether or not they were going to have the service continued or discontinued or whether or not different firms could engage in cutthroat competition and run one another into bankruptcy, thereby leaving communities without any services. This sort of thing has been going on year after year and certainly I and, as I mentioned earlier, the long-time member for Comox-Alberni, Mr. A. W. Neill, recognized the danger of the situation.
In particular, during the period since the end of the Second World War when air traffic entered into coastal transportation as a major factor, steamer services have been disrupted without notice to those being served. This has meant disruption of services which have provided the necessary communication to keep a community operating. It has made very difficult and complicated the work of the people charged with the responsibility for the transportation of the mails along the coast of British Columbia.
fMr. Barnett.]
I could go on and enumerate the kind of problems which have resulted in many communities receiving poorer service today than they had 50 years ago.
I have a letter before me which has reached my office, mailed from Winter Harbour on April 12 of this year, which touches on this very important situation. I should like to read part of this to the House:
I have been informed this morning that the Island Tug & Barge Company that services the village of Winter Harbour and this logging operation-
By the way, this letter is written by the proprietor of the logging operation.
-will drop their weekly freight and mail service and replace it with a once every second week service.
The Winter Harbour Post Office is serviced by this barge and this announcement will mean we here go back 30 years in postal service.
The reason given for the dropping of Winter Harbour by Mr. Sterling Beek, traffic manager of Island Tug & Barge is that they "must meet their deadline at Port Alice for the pulp load".
The village of Quatsino is also dropped from the once a week service... I have called the Rayonier Company-
That is the company which operates the Port Alice pulp mill.
-to help us in any way they can but felt you might be able to exert some form of pressure to assist both villages.
The fact that this particular Bill No. C-5 has now come up for second reading gives me an opportunity publicly to put on the record of this House the problems faced by the people of these two communities, creating a situation from which they have no appeal except to their Member of Parliament. There is no body of any kind to which they can go which has any authority to deal with this kind of situation.
The letter goes on to say:
The service of this company has been excellent and we fail to see why at this late date they would make a sudden change.
When the roads come to this area we will have alternate routes but we are quite helpless to do anything but si* by and watch this company eliminate two small villages from a decent freight and mail service.
I suppose I have had dozens of letters of a similar nature to this one during the years I have been a member of this House. I have had telegrams couched in frantic terms informing me that, effective the following week, there would be no service of any kind to bring in mail or supplies. I have previously tried to argue that this is a situation which is simply not good enough. I have always made it clear that it was not my view that any private
April 30. 1965

transportation company should be required indefinitely to maintain a service which is completely uneconomical to operate. If there are situations where services are sufficiently essential, then we have our system of subventions under the Canadian Maritime Commission, which of course is operative in certain instances on the coast of British Columbia. But it is only when a subvention under the Canadian Maritime Commission does become operative for a particular service that the company providing the service has any public responsibility or accepts any public guarantee that it will maintain that service, and maintain it according to an announced schedule of rates.
I am sure that no Member in this House, Mr. Speaker, expects that all the water carrier services, through the operation of the Canadian Maritime Commission, require or need subventions, but I do submit that people in these communities should have some court of appeal to go to when the companies which have accepted responsibility for providing these services suddenly, without notice, decide to change them in the drastic manner that I have been attempting to describe.
I also suggest that in my view there should be some kind of protection afforded to people who invest their money in ships to provide such services. Quite frankly, I have found it hard to understand why over the years the major shipping companies, at least on the British Columbia coast, have registered their objection to the proposals advanced in this Bill and, as I understand it, originally registered objection to the attempt of the former Member of Parliament for Comox-Alberni, Mr. A. W. Neill, to have this particular phrase removed from the original Transport Act.
As I recall the discussion we had in the House last year, at least one of the British Columbia members who spoke registered some concern at the effect of my Bill, which would bring under this kind of jurisdiction and licensing the many operations which are conducted under some form of contract where goods are carried in bulk for private companies. I refer to the transportation and movement of such things as booms of logs, rafts of logs, log barges and the transportation of what is now becoming a major element of traffic along the coast, namely pulp chips, and in some cases the carriage of ore in bulk.
I should like to point out that in both Part II and Part III of the Act specific reference is made to the fact that carriage of goods in bulk does not come under the licensing pro-

visions of the Act. While that provision may not appear in the particular amendment which I have moved, if anybody wishes to refer to the Act which I propose to amend and is prepared to read the definition section dealing with bulk goods, he will immediately be aware of the fact that the purpose of my Bill is to provide that there be some form of public regulation of those people who are, in effect, public carriers; and that is all I seek to accomplish by the amendments.

As I listened to the hon. Member I wondered what was bothering him, in connection with the transportation of goods in British Columbia, which led him to believe that certain regulations should be applied from Ottawa to this booming traffic. Does the hon. Member believe, for example, that there are delays involved? Let me deal for a moment with that question. As the years have gone by, the network of roads on Vancouver Island has been vastly improved, and both my hon. friend and I would agree heartily with that. They have been extended mile after mile. Not only have they been extended up the island, but they have been extended across the island and even now are beginning to reach out to the west coast which now, for the first time, from day to day, though not all year round, can be reached by automobile traffic. So roads are coming to the aid of many of these areas which heretofore did not have any access except by sea for the bringing in of their mail and their goods unless, of course, they had them transported by air.
May I remind my hon. friend that the ferry service back and forth across the straits has also been improved over the years. May I remind him also that the van or truck service moving back and forth across the Straits of Georgia on the ferries is now about as efficient as anywhere in the country. Therefore, with the improved network of roads, with the extension of roads up and down and across the island and with the improvement of the ferry service and the trucking service to the island, many more points in a fortunate island are being provided with increasingly efficient transportation facilities.
Let me deal with the growth of air transport in the Province of British Columbia. Nowhere in this country, and perhaps nowhere on the North American continent, is an area better served by air than British Columbia. Mail is taken by seaplane and flying boat from Vancouver airport to many of the waterways up and down the coast. The seaplane delivery of mail and small cargo has now made quite unnecessary the carrying of much of the traffic slowly and laboriously by log boom or by barge. The delivery of mail to logging camps, fishing camps and so on up and down the coast of British Columbia has been speeded up.
With regard to lack of competition I want to ask my friend this question. In an open market such as this, is there any lack of competition in providing him with efficient
Transport
service? Are there excessive charges in an area where competitors have ample freedom to operate? I want to say to him that it is an area in which there is little regulation and in which we find real, free enterprise at work. Where this is so, what do we find? We find one of the best developed transportation systems by land, by air, by sea, by road and by rail that can be found anywhere in the whole of Canada. Why would my hon. friend want to poke his finger into that area which is regulated so well by competition, and introduce subventions which would be charged to the taxpayers of Canada? Why would he want to bring it under the control of a regulatory body 2,000 miles away?
I cannot for a moment subscribe to the Bill that the hon. Member now has before the House if it would result in those things being done. The history of the people of British Columbia has been one of going into the wilderness, and they have never had to move out of such areas because of a lack of transportation. In fact, what has happened up and down the coast of British Columbia is that the expansion of transportation facilities has enabled them to do many things in an enormously difficult territory with what seems to be incredible ease. I suggest to the hon. Member that if there is any place where free competition should be allowed to reign and which regulatory bodies should leave alone, it is in the area of the free flow of transportation in the Province of British Columbia.

stands of the finest timber in Canada, and in the summertime it is a vacationland which I think is pretty hard to beat.
That part of Canada, however, has peculiar problems because it is still a frontierland. From my own experience I know that charts of the West Coast of Canada showing what the coastline is have only recently come into the hands of the public, and only a very few years ago when I was travelling back and forth on these waters there were large parts of the shoreline which were shown in dotted lines as not having even been surveyed at that time, only 10 years ago. In the area on the West Coast of British Columbia now under discussion there are a fair number of smaller communities which are not self-supporting, however important they may be to our economy. These communities cannot yet depend upon roads for communication purposes and, as we all know, communication by air is an expensive proposition. They must rely in large part upon water transportation.
I know that there are few enough freedoms today, and freedom of the seas is something which is quite close to my heart. But I also believe that with that freedom goes a responsibility, and in the absence of competition from other means of transportation up and down our coast I think that these small communities need the protection which only legislation such as this can provide them. Unless the transportation companies, which are admittedly in business to make money, are charged by the country with the responsibility of servicing, not only the more lucrative portions of their routes but also the smaller communities which may not produce much in the way of revenue to the transportation companies, I think we are failing in our duty with regard to the development of our West Coast, a duty which can only be fulfilled when these small communities are provided with the service that will enable them to expand.

I think it is only right that we should do the same thing for the isolated communities in British Columbia in order to provide them with transportation and communications.

Mr. Speaker, on entering the debate on Bill No. C-5 I wish to state that I could not contribute anything specifically to the regional problem of British Columbia. Indeed, wherever shipping may be operating for captive users, I think this principle put forward by the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) could be accepted. I accept, in principle, this thought which I believe the hon. Member wished to express in this Bill. The problem that confronts me, however, is that it should not be done on a piecemeal basis across the country. I feel the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) should be concerned with the application of policy generally throughout Canada. I am sure all of us have shared in the observance of the various methods and procedures adopted by countries to regulate monopolies and to make certain, as I said earlier, that public necessity and convenience is fully protected. We see public utility boards regulating telephone rates and railway rates because, obviously, you have a monopoly situation which could only exist under the operation of proper public utility boards who can analyse all the cost factors essential to a determination of fair and reasonable rates, or the extension of services.

We know there are a lot of shortcomings and we start off with a Bill that seems to take care of them, but then we find in turn that it does not cover many situations that exist. Obviously there will have to be some real approach to the question of railway legislation.
During the course of the Committee meetings I was struck by the necessity to be alert in many situations where you have captive users across the country. You can have a captive user of an air line, of a shipping line, and indeed of a railway, and there must be many situations in Canada where the Department or the Minister of Transport might give some thought to a single agency regulating rates and services in the entire transport field. I would like to suggest the advisability of bringing all three, ship, rail and air, under one board, because it was quite clear in the Committee meetings that what the proposed Bill was trying to do was to provide a procedure whereby a board could identify areas of adequate competition to ensure protection of the public.
Then again you get into those situations where there are not exactly agreements between the large suppliers of transport but where you wonder if, in their mutual interests, there is not a tacit agreement which may require examination by a Government regulating authority.

April 30, 1965
Transport
What I am saying is that the principle on which this bill is founded requires greater concentration of thought on the part of the Minister and his Department, and we should look at what it attempts to achieve from a national policy point of view. It would be a shame if we were to deal with a relatively small section of the problem in B.C. without applying the policy generally throughout Canada. Such a bill should be on a nationwide basis and be applicable wherever the same circumstances arise.
There would be a great deal of merit in examining the wisdom of establishing a single, national authority to regulate rates and services in the three transportation fields of air, railway and steamship lines. If that approach were taken I feel confident that the numerous attempts of the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) to achieve what he is trying to achieve in B.C. would be successful. On such short notice I cannot imagine all the kinds of situations that will arise when you try to distinguish between strictly competitive forms of transport, and monopoly situations, but some Government agency should exist to do this.
In the Atlantic region we are concerned that the proposed railway Bill suggests that the Board of Transport Commissioners would be able to regulate rates after some figure of 150 per cent above operating costs. We recognize some thought must have been given to this figure, but we want greater explanation why 150 per cent was selected in preference to 100 per cent, 75 per cent or even 200 per
cent, before we can feel fully confident that this kind of policy should be supported.
We should press for the establishment of a Federal body that would regulate all three transportation services. Until we have that we will continue to add to our difficulties. Governments must be constantly alert wherever there is a monopoly situation.
Sometimes I wonder whether the C.B.C., operating as it is as a Government agency, and being confronted with a single C.T.V. station chain is in a truly competitive position. If there were two private C.T.V. station chains then we would have a competitive position, but we have not yet really polished the apple of administration to the extent that we can say that the C.B.C. and the single C.T.V. chain of stations are strictly competitive and therefore need no regulation. I think a very close and detailed examination along these lines might reveal some interesting facts.

Prime Minister of Cda Ottawa Ont=: Further to my telegram of April seven, local opinion is strongly opposed to continuing transfers of Air Canada personnel. This is felt to be violation of your promise to freeze situation pending receipt of Thompson Commission Report. Continuation of these moves is bound to prejudice policy decisions your Government must take when Thompson Commission Reports submitted to you. Earnestly request Transport Minister Pickersgill come to Winnipeg soonest to clarify situation with unions municipalities and provincial government representatives =
Duff Roblin
Prime Minister's Office April 30, 1965
Hon. Duff Roblin,
Premier of Manitoba,
Winnipeg, Man.
Your telegram regarding transfers of Air Canada personnel received. You suggest transfers are felt to be violation of my promise to freeze situation pending receipt of Thompson Commission Report.
You surely recall the answer I gave you on March 21, 1964, to the question put to me by you about employment at Air Canada Maintenance Base. Your question was as follows:
Question: In terms of your statements in Parliament, what undertakings do you consider you have given about the maintenance
of employment at the Winnipeg TCA overhaul base?"
Answer: "I said in Parliament on December 17 last year:
''It is the policy of the government to do everything possible to maintain employment at the TCA base in Winnipeg and, if possible, to increase it."
So far as TCA is concerned, this means that the base will continue to be used for the overhaul of Viscount aircraft as long as these aircraft are in service.
As far as the government is concerned, it means further that we will do everything we can to ensure that other aircraft work is available in Winnipeg so that the eventual withdrawal of the Viscounts is at least balanced by new activities.
This policy should not be interpreted as a guarantee that each particular job now filled in Winnipeg will continue indefinitely. Normal changes in technology and work methods, and the provisions of seniority rules between employer and employee, may lead to the disappearance or transfer of particular jobs. A dynamic industry cannot be frozen into a particular employment pattern.
My undertakings mean that there will be no transfer of work from Winnipeg by deliberate policy. On the contrary, the policy is to do our utmost to secure enough aircraft work to maintain or improve the present employment level."
Information provided by Air Canada indicates that all transfers made or in contemplation are being made pursuant to collective agreements in strict accord with my answer given to you and with all subsequent statements made on behalf of this government.
L. B. Pearson.
Monday, May 3, 1965
